text:
The Case for Keeping Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years a familiar argument resurfaces. Keyboards are everywhere, children will type for most of their working lives, and so the hours spent teaching them to loop and link letters on lined paper look like a relic. Several education systems have already acted on that logic and dropped joined writing from their requirements. I think that is a mistake. Primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it properly, with time, structure and expectation. The reasons are not sentimental. They rest on what handwriting does for children's thinking, on what it offers the child who struggles, and on the simple fact that a skill taught early is cheap while a skill left untaught is expensive to acquire later.

Begin with the strongest objection, because it deserves a fair hearing. Typing is a vital skill, and most adult writing is now done on a screen. A child who leaves primary school unable to touch type is handicapped. All of that is true. But it does not follow that handwriting must be sacrificed. The two skills are not rivals competing for a single slot in the timetable. Handwriting practice, done well, takes perhaps a few short sessions each week. Keyboard skills can be taught alongside it, and in many schools they already are. The choice presented to us is a false one. What we are really deciding is whether a modest and well-understood part of the curriculum is worth keeping, and I think the evidence says it is.

The first argument concerns how children learn to write at all. Forming letters by hand is a slow, effortful, physical act. That slowness is useful. When a young child traces the shape of a letter, the movement, the sight of the mark and the sound of the letter are tied together in memory. Researchers who study early literacy have repeatedly found that children who write letters by hand tend to recognise and remember them better than children who only press keys. A keyboard asks a child to find a letter among dozens that all look and feel alike. A pencil asks the child to build the letter from nothing. Building is harder, and that difficulty is exactly what makes the learning stick. It would be odd to remove the harder route in the early years and then wonder why spelling and letter recognition are weaker.

Joined writing in particular earns its place within this picture. Printing letters one at a time means lifting the pen after every character, which breaks each word into disconnected fragments. Joining letters turns a word into a single movement. The hand learns the word as a pattern, and many teachers report that this helps spelling, because the child feels the sequence of letters as a rhythm rather than a list. A cursive word also has a clear boundary. Children who print often leave uneven gaps, and letters such as b and d, which are mirror images in print, become easier to tell apart when each has its own distinct entry and exit stroke. That last point matters most for reversal, the stubborn habit of writing letters backwards that troubles many young writers.

The second argument is about fluency and the load on the working mind. A child writing a story has to juggle an enormous amount. There are ideas to hold, sentences to build, words to spell and punctuation to place. If forming each letter still demands conscious effort, less attention is left for everything else. Fluent handwriting frees the mind. Children who write quickly and legibly produce longer and richer work, because the physical act no longer gets in the way of the thought. Joined writing, once mastered, is faster than printing. The pen stays on the page and the hand moves with a continuous flow. For a ten-year-old facing a timed exam, a note-taking task or a long piece of writing, that speed is a real advantage. It is no accident that so many secondary schools and examining bodies still expect handwritten work, and that students who cannot write fast and legibly lose marks through no fault of their understanding.

Here lies a point that critics of cursive often overlook. Handwriting is not going away in the places that matter most to a child's progress. Exams are still written by hand in most countries. Classroom notes, quick workings in mathematics, labels on diagrams and notes in the margin of a book are all handwritten, even in schools full of tablets. A child who has never been taught an efficient, legible hand will struggle in all of these, and the struggle will be invisible to the adults around them, who will see only a messy page and assume carelessness. Teaching joined writing early is how we make sure that every child, not just the naturally neat ones, has a reliable tool for the situations where a screen is unavailable or unwelcome.

That brings me to fairness, which for me is the heart of the case. Children arrive at school with very different advantages. Some have a tablet at home and a parent who sits with them to practise letters. Others have neither. If schools stop teaching handwriting as a structured skill, the children with support at home will learn it anyway, from parents, tutors and their own enthusiasm, while the children without that support will be left with a ragged, self-taught scrawl that holds them back. Explicit teaching is the great equaliser. It gives every child the same method, the same practice and the same chance to write comfortably. Dropping it does not remove the skill from the world. It simply hands the skill to the families who can afford to teach it privately.

There is a particular benefit for children with certain learning differences, which is worth stating carefully because the picture is mixed. Some children with dyslexia or dyspraxia find handwriting hard, and some of them are helped enormously by keyboards. But many specialists also recommend a consistent, joined script for these same children, precisely because it reduces the number of decisions the hand must make. A single flowing movement for each word is more predictable than a stop-start sequence of separate marks. The right response to difficulty is support and flexibility, not abolition. A school can teach cursive to everyone and still allow a keyboard for the child who truly needs one.

There is also something to be said for the ordinary pleasures and uses of the skill. A handwritten card, a letter to a grandparent, a diary kept in a child's own flowing script, a signature that is recognisably theirs. These are small things, but they are part of what it means to be a literate person, and they connect children to a long tradition of written culture. A child who cannot read joined-up writing also cannot read old family letters, historical documents or a teacher's comments on their own work. Illiteracy in cursive is a quiet kind of cut-off, and it is easily prevented.

Some will say that this is nostalgia dressed up as argument. I would answer that nostalgia cuts the other way. The truly faddish position is to assume that a new technology makes an old skill obsolete without checking what that skill was doing. Handwriting has survived the printing press, the typewriter and the word processor because it does several jobs at once. It trains the hand, anchors letters in memory, supports spelling, builds fluency and gives every child a tool that works without power or a connection. A school that drops it saves little time and loses much.

None of this means going back to the rigid drills of the past, with children copying the same line of loops for an hour and being shamed for a wobbly tail on a letter g. Good handwriting teaching is short, regular and encouraging. A few minutes a day, a clear and simple model script, attention to posture and pencil grip, and plenty of praise for legibility rather than perfection. Teachers should be trained to do this well, and schools should protect the time for it. Done like that, it costs little and returns a great deal.

So my answer is yes. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. They should teach it alongside keyboard skills rather than instead of them, they should teach it kindly, and they should teach it to every child. The skill helps children learn letters, spell words, write quickly, sit exams and take part in a literate culture, and it does so most fairly when the school provides it rather than leaving it to chance. A curriculum is a statement about what we think every child deserves to be able to do. A fluent, legible, personal hand still belongs on that list.
